title: Word Pairs That Read Both Ways
statement:
You get a list of distinct lowercase words. A pair of indexes [i, j] with i ≠ j is good when the glued string words[i] + words[j] reads the same forwards and backwards.

Return every good pair. Order matters inside a pair ([i, j] and [j, i] are different pairs), but the list of pairs may be in any order. The empty word may appear.

examples.why: "abba", "baab", "aba" and "aba". "a" + "ab" = "aab" is not good, so direction matters.
"racecar" works, "carrace" does not. The empty word only pairs with words that are palindromes already.
"aa" and "b" are palindromes, so each pairs with the empty word on either side. "aab" and "baa" are not good.

hints: Checking every pair costs O(n² · L). Instead, for one word, ask: what would the other word have to look like?
If w + v is a palindrome and v is the shorter one, then v must be the reverse of the start of w, and the rest of w must be a palindrome on its own.

Put every reversed word in a hash map. For each word, try every cut into prefix + suffix: if the suffix is a palindrome, look up the prefix (v goes after w); if the prefix is a palindrome, look up the suffix (v goes before w).

explain.intuition:
Take a good pair w + v where w is at least as long as v. Reading from the outside in, v must mirror the beginning of w, and whatever is left over in the middle of w must be a palindrome by itself. So cut w into prefix + suffix: the pair is good when suffix is a palindrome and v equals reverse(prefix). The case where v goes first is the mirror image: prefix is a palindrome and v = reverse(suffix).

A word of length L has only L + 1 cuts, and a hash map of reversed words answers "is there such a v?" instantly. That turns n² comparisons into n · L² work.
steps: Map every reversed word to its index.
For each word w at index i, and each cut k from 0 to len(w), split into prefix = w[:k] and suffix = w[k:].
If suffix is a palindrome and the map has prefix at index j ≠ i, record [i, j].
If k > 0, prefix is a palindrome and the map has suffix at j ≠ i, record [j, i].
pitfalls: Recording the same pair twice when two words are exact reverses of each other. The k > 0 condition on the second check prevents that.
Pairing a word with itself when it is its own reverse, like "aba". Always check j ≠ i.
Forgetting the empty word. It pairs with every palindrome on both sides, which the cut at k = 0 and k = len(w) handles naturally.

solutions.title: Check every ordered pair
solutions.idea: Glue every two different words in both orders and test the result.

solutions.title: Reversed-word map and every cut
solutions.idea: Store reversed words in a map. For each cut of each word, a palindromic half plus a matching reversed other half gives a pair.

followups: Store the reversed words in a trie instead of a hash map. What does each lookup save?
Words can now repeat. How do you adjust the map and the j ≠ i rule?
